Extinction Event. A period of rapid loss of biodiversity in which a significant fraction of the world's species disappear in a relatively short geological time. Earth has experienced five major extinction events over the past five hundred and forty million years. Each reshaped ecosystems and opened ecological niches for survivors.

The Big Five mass extinction events are the Ordovician-Silurian, four hundred and fifty million years ago. Late Devonian, three hundred and seventy-five million years ago. Permian-Triassic, two hundred and fifty-two million years ago. Triassic-Jurassic, two hundred million years ago. And Cretaceous-Paleogene, sixty-six million years ago. These span the entire history of complex multicellular life.

The Permian-Triassic extinction is called the Great Dying. It eliminated roughly ninety-six percent of marine species and seventy percent of terrestrial vertebrate species, making it the most severe extinction known. The Cretaceous-Paleogene extinction, sixty-six million years ago, wiped out non-avian dinosaurs. A massive asteroid impact near present-day Mexico is the primary cause.

Synapsids, which are proto-mammals, were devastated by the Permian extinction. But lineages survived to eventually evolve into modern mammals. Causes of extinction events include asteroid impacts, massive volcanism, climate shifts, ocean acidification, and disruption of food chains.

Extinction opens ecological opportunity by freeing resources. After non-avian dinosaurs died, mammals diversified rapidly and eventually dominated terrestrial ecosystems, filling the vacant niches. Modern biodiversity loss is sometimes called the Sixth Extinction, driven by human activity—habitat destruction, climate change, and pollution—rather than natural catastrophes. It occurs at rates comparable to or exceeding past mass extinction events.

Dinosaurs were eliminated by the K-Pg extinction event sixty-six million years ago. Synapsids were severely impacted by the Permian-Triassic extinction but survived. Extinction events are key turning points in evolutionary history. The Permian period was home to the most severe extinction event in Earth's history. The Cretaceous period ended with the K-Pg extinction that killed non-avian dinosaurs. And paleontology is the science that studies extinction through the fossil record.
